title: The Breakdown (1)

jokes.text: Hank misreads the 'Applause' sign as 'Applesauce' then immediately corrects himself
jokes.setup: Hank is warming up the studio audience by referring to the cue sign
jokes.punchline: He announces it says 'Applesauce,' then casually corrects it — as if the misread were a conscious bit rather than genuine incompetence
jokes.explanation: A nice cold open character beat — Hank's hapless attempt to seem in control. It's quick and efficient, character-specific enough to work as a first impression of Hank's oblivious showbiz persona, but not especially original.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That sign says 'Applesauce.' No, no, no. I'm kidding. It says 'applause.'

jokes.text: Announcer intro: '...and now, because it's a condition of his probation, Larry Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Standard late-night show announcer introduction of the host, following a list of guests including Hank's self-introduction
jokes.punchline: 'Because it's a condition of his probation' — subverts the flattering intro formula with a criminal implication
jokes.explanation: Economical and structurally elegant — the announcer intro is a sacred TV ritual, and inserting 'condition of his probation' is a perfectly placed subversion. It's meta (the show satirizing the genre it inhabits), quotable, and efficiently delivered. The juxtaposition with the straight list of guest names earns it. High economy and structure scores.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: and now, because it's a condition of his probation, Larry Sanders!

jokes.text: Larry's Clinton/Redford deficit joke: 'For a million dollars, he'd let Robert Redford sleep with Hillary'
jokes.setup: Clinton announced a new plan to end the deficit
jokes.punchline: The plan involves selling access to Hillary — positioning the First Lady as a commodity in a sex joke
jokes.explanation: Standard early-90s late-night political sex joke. Could have been written for any host. The Clinton-Hillary-sex angle was extremely well-worn by 1993. It functions as verisimilitude — showing us what Larry's monologue looks like — but the joke itself is weak. Low originality and earned scores.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: He said for a million dollars, he'd let Robert Redford sleep with Hillary.

jokes.text: 'If Robert Redford has to pay a million dollars to get laid... Do I need to finish this thought? Imagine what Hank must have to pay.'
jokes.setup: Follow-up to the Redford/Clinton joke — Larry builds on the premise that even a handsome movie star has trouble
jokes.punchline: Pivots to roast Hank, using mock-rhetorical 'Do I need to finish this thought?' as false pause before the real punchline
jokes.explanation: Better than the preceding monologue joke because it has a two-beat structure and character specificity — the sidekick-as-butt-of-joke is a classic late-night dynamic. The 'Do I need to finish this thought?' feint adds structure. Character integration is good because this kind of Larry-brutalizes-Hank dynamic defines their relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If Robert Redford has to pay a million dollars to get laid... Do I need to finish this thought? Imagine what Hank must have to pay.

jokes.text: Larry is watching TV, tells his wife on the phone he's watching Bonanza — 'That is not Hank. That is Hoss.'
jokes.setup: Larry is clearly watching his own show while on the phone with Jeannie, insisting he isn't
jokes.punchline: When she apparently notices Hank on screen, he denies it's Hank by claiming it's the Bonanza character Hoss — the implication being Hank resembles the large, dim cowboy character
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's first genuinely great joke. It layers multiple comedic truths: Larry's pathological self-involvement (watching his own show while fighting with his wife), his contempt for Hank (comparing him to Hoss), and his transparent lying. The Hoss reference is hyper-specific and deeply character-integrated — only Larry Sanders would reach for that particular Bonanza insult. Highly quotable and reveals character elegantly. The economy is exceptional: four words ('That is Hoss') carry enormous freight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I am not watching my show right now. I'm watching Bonanza. That is not Hank. That is Hoss.

jokes.text: Larry's phone call with Jeannie: a long series of 'Uh-huh. Right. Uh-huh.' as she apparently lists his failings, punctuated by 'Hey, that is more of a quirk, don't you think?'
jokes.setup: Larry and his estranged wife are arguing on the phone; he said he'd 'go into some areas she never considered'
jokes.punchline: Instead of defending himself, he just absorbs the list with repeated 'uh-huhs' and tries to reclassify his worst traits as mere 'quirks' — twice
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed cringe sequence that works on one-sided phone call comedy. The escalating 'uh-huhs' paired with the weak rebuttal 'that is more of a quirk' is perfectly Shandling — Larry has no real defense, just denial management. The repetition of 'quirk' makes it a mini-running gag within the scene. Deeply character-integrated: Larry's pathological inability to accept criticism is the show's DNA.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Why do you put her through?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Larry, you called her.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, that's right.

jokes.text: 'Why do you put her through?' / 'Larry, you called her.' / 'Oh, that's right.'
jokes.setup: Larry complains 'All this woman does is berate me' after hanging up
jokes.punchline: Beverly points out he called her; Larry's oblivious 'Oh, that's right' reveals he'd forgotten he initiated the call
jokes.explanation: Three lines that deliver maximum character insight. Larry's victimhood narrative collapses the instant Beverly states a simple fact, and his guileless 'Oh, that's right' shows he isn't even aware of his own behavior. Perfect economy. Beverly's flat delivery makes it land harder. This is the kind of micro-beat the show excels at.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do I have trouble prioritizing emotional commitments?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Oh, please, don't ask me. I haven't had a healthy relationship since junior high.

jokes.text: 'Do I have trouble prioritizing emotional commitments?' / 'Oh, please, don't ask me. I haven't had a healthy relationship since junior high.' / 'Oh. Wow. Well, let's stick to me today.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Beverly for a candid self-assessment right after proving he can't prioritize
jokes.punchline: Beverly's unexpected overshare about her own romantic failures, immediately cut off by Larry's dismissive 'Well, let's stick to me today' — making his narcissism the joke
jokes.explanation: 'Let's stick to me today' is a perfect Larry Sanders line — it's so nakedly self-absorbed that it circles back to being charming. Beverly's brief overshare is a great setup: it humanizes her while setting up Larry's dismissal. The line is highly quotable and could stand alone as a character thesis statement.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, let's stick to me today.

jokes.text: Larry reads the Letterman article aloud, muttering and fast-forwarding through the parts he doesn't care about with 'blah blah blah'
jokes.setup: Larry says he wants Beverly to 'listen to this' — implying an important piece of information is coming
jokes.punchline: He reads impatiently, skipping most of the article until he finds the one data point that confirms his anxiety about being beaten by a younger-skewing Letterman
jokes.explanation: A functional character comedy beat showing Larry's tunnel-vision insecurity. The 'blah blah blah' is a nice performance note but the joke is more observational setup than punchline — it pays off more in the context of his obsessive Letterman fixation throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Jesus! Are you laying in your own puke?

jokes.text: Larry muttering to himself: 'Just what I need — someone taking more of the younger audience.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just read that Letterman will pull younger viewers
jokes.punchline: The muttered self-pity, delivered as an aside, is both pathetic and funny — a man spiraling over ratings while his marriage ends
jokes.explanation: A quiet character beat — funny because of the tonal contrast between the gravity of his divorce and the petty ratings anxiety. Works better in context than in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Who are they? It's a mystery.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They don't need to be a mystery to me, Artie. I'm the host.

jokes.text: 'Jesus! Are you laying in your own puke?' (Artie's entrance, apparently disheveled)
jokes.setup: Artie arrives at Larry's office; Larry's shocked reaction implies Artie looks terrible
jokes.punchline: The blunt, alarmed question from Larry — and Artie's total non-reaction to it, immediately pivoting to asking about the trades — suggests this is not unusual for Artie
jokes.explanation: The joke is Artie's completely unfazed pivot to business as usual ('Do you have the trades?') — a man who apparently showed up in a state of physical distress and whose only concern is industry news. Great character-integrated visual comedy. Artie's imperturbability in the face of chaos is one of his defining traits.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'll tell you who got nominated. Letterman, Saturday Night Live, and I'll bet you Billy Crystal hosting the Academy Awards. Am I right? What's the other one? A Jackie Mason Hanukkah, Artie?

jokes.text: 'We have an excellent show tonight — supermodel Kathy Ireland and two mystery guests.' / 'Who are they?' / 'It's a mystery.' / 'They don't need to be a mystery to me, Artie. I'm the host.'
jokes.setup: Artie promotes the night's guests to Larry
jokes.punchline: Artie's deadpan 'It's a mystery' treats 'mystery guest' as a literal condition, forcing Larry to point out the obvious absurdity of being kept in the dark about his own show
jokes.explanation: A tight three-exchange bit that lands because Artie's deadpan is total — he gives Larry no way out. The comedy is in the power dynamic: the producer withholding information from the host of his own show, and the host having to articulate why that's absurd. Good economy and strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Walk it off?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Cancel. Move on. Why don't I just put ice on it? It's a marriage, for god's sakes!

jokes.text: 'I'm not going to the bathroom for two hours. Let me see them.' (about the trades with Emmy nominations)
jokes.setup: Larry demands to see the trades; Artie is stalling
jokes.punchline: Artie's excuse is that he hasn't been able to go to the bathroom yet — a non-sequitur justification for not reading the trades that doubles as an oddly personal overshare
jokes.explanation: Funny in a low-key way — the specificity of 'two hours' and the bathroom detail makes it feel real. Artie using bodily functions as a stalling tactic is very Artie. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They're out there. You don't need to check. Artie was selling them like there's no tomorrow. They must be there, or he wouldn't be in here saying there's hot towels. They must be out there very close by. There's hot towels out there. I could tell.

jokes.text: 'Bastards. Shit.' — Larry's reaction to learning the Emmy nominations don't include him
jokes.setup: Larry told Artie not to tell him the nominations — 'Don't tell me'
jokes.punchline: Artie's face apparently reveals the news before saying anything; Larry's immediate 'Bastards. Shit.' is the perfect paranoid response to a confirmation of his worst fear
jokes.explanation: Two words deliver perfect character comedy. The staccato rhythm of 'Bastards. Shit.' is funny — the second expletive is the escalation. It's economical and character-specific: Larry's explosive but private grievances are his mode.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I thought you were talking about the Emmy nominations. Oh, screw her! She was always trying to drive a wedge between Larry and me.

jokes.text: 'I'll bet you Billy Crystal hosting the Academy Awards.' / 'What's the other one?' / 'A Jackie Mason Hanukkah, Artie?'
jokes.setup: Larry is predicting the Emmy nominees: Letterman, SNL, Billy Crystal hosting the Oscars
jokes.punchline: Artie asks about the fourth slot; Larry's contemptuous 'A Jackie Mason Hanukkah, Artie?' implies the fourth nominee is equally obvious and lowbrow — a dismissal in the form of a Jewish comedy special that would never beat him
jokes.explanation: Industry-insider comedy — funny to anyone who knows Jackie Mason's niche appeal. The specificity of 'Hanukkah' as a marker for cable-ghetto programming is sharp. Larry's scornful rhetorical question mode is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: We'd hit the bar at the Bel Air hotel, work a little skirt.

jokes.text: 'Cable shows should be a different category. We're slipping.' / 'Absolutely not.' / 'I'm not blaming you.'
jokes.setup: Larry is rationalizing why they didn't get an Emmy nomination
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not blaming you' immediately after Artie denies slippage — a passive-aggressive move that functions as a direct accusation dressed as absolution
jokes.explanation: Compact and character-true — Larry's 'I'm not blaming you' is exactly how a narcissist expresses blame. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Jerry van dyke. Fuck him.

jokes.text: 'Cancel. Move on.' — Artie doubles down with TV-production language applied to the marriage
jokes.setup: Larry protests 'Walk it off? It's a marriage, for god's sake!'
jokes.punchline: Artie pivots to show business metaphor: 'Cancel. Move on.' — treating the marriage like a struggling television program
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best standalone line. 'Cancel. Move on.' is a show-business producer's vocabulary applied to a human relationship — and from Artie, it's not callousness but his genuine philosophy. The economy is extraordinary: two words, two beats, total character encapsulation. The joke works because Artie means it literally and emotionally simultaneously. Justifies the 8+ score: it's genuinely exceptional craft — comparable in density to the 'walk it off' anchor but with the added layer of the TV-production metaphor making it entirely specific to this world.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This towel isn't even hot!

jokes.text: 'Walk it off.' / 'Walk it off?' / 'Cancel. Move on.' / 'Why don't I just put ice on it? It's a marriage, for God's sakes!'
jokes.setup: Larry is expressing genuine grief about his failed marriage; Artie is trying to be supportive
jokes.punchline: Artie's sports-medicine approach to emotional trauma — 'Walk it off,' 'Cancel. Move on.' — is comically insufficient; Larry's sarcastic 'Why don't I just put ice on it?' escalates the absurdity perfectly
jokes.explanation: This exchange perfectly captures both characters simultaneously. Artie's gruff emotional minimalism — treating heartbreak like a sprained ankle — and Larry's genuine wounded indignation are both funny and true. 'Cancel. Move on.' is a spectacular three-word summation of Artie's life philosophy. The escalation to 'put ice on it' gives Larry rare comic agency. Very strong character integration for both.

dialogue.line: Phoenix?
They're dropping you for Chevy Chase.
You're kidding.
Hard to believe, isn't it?

jokes.text: Larry and Artie both start purring when told Kathy Ireland is trying on wardrobe
jokes.setup: A PA delivers the news that supermodel Kathy Ireland is trying on wardrobe — a professional update
jokes.punchline: Both Larry and Artie respond with simultaneous cat-like purring, then Larry says 'as attractive as you make it sound' — two grown industry professionals reduced to adolescence
jokes.explanation: The shared purring is a visual/physical comedy beat that works because it's synchronized — both men doing it simultaneously reveals their arrested development. 'Oh, as attractive as you make it sound' is dry and self-aware. The joke is also structurally interesting because Larry then immediately has to pivot back to 'focus.'

dialogue.speaker: Kathy Ireland
dialogue.line: They're great. Open-toed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Mine are closed-toed-- I like all your shoes.

jokes.text: Artie and Larry both start purring/eagerly responding to news that Kathy Ireland is trying on wardrobe
jokes.setup: A staff member interrupts the grief conversation to say Kathy Ireland is doing costume changes
jokes.punchline: Both men — one in the middle of a marriage breakdown conversation — immediately drop all emotional weight and respond with animal eagerness ('both purring'), making the transition from grief to horniness instantaneous
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom gear-shift gag — emotional sincerity punctured by base instinct. The stage direction '[both purring]' suggests a physical comedy moment. Works because the transition is so abrupt and shameless.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Until we get this show on track, I have no dick.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No dick? Check.

jokes.text: Artie's speech to get Larry to go see Kathy Ireland: 'Supermodel, costume changes, fittings... anything could happen.' Larry: 'Oh, as attractive as you make it sound.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to motivate Larry to come see Kathy Ireland by listing the scenario's 'selling points'
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, sardonic 'Oh, as attractive as you make it sound' — a rare moment of Larry being the straight man to Artie's absurd enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: A small but well-delivered ironic beat. Larry's sarcasm here is mild but works as a rhythm beat in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Jesus, he's dipping into the toilet. I agree. Why didn't we get the Buttafuocos on? They turned us down. Good. They're not right for the show anyway. I agree. Fucking Koppel blurs the line. My god, no, it's not right.

jokes.text: Larry asks Beverly to get Jeannie on the phone, Beverly refuses ('Uh-uh. No.'), Larry immediately says 'Good. Get me a hot towel.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Beverly to call Jeannie, implying he needs emotional contact
jokes.punchline: Beverly's flat refusal; Larry's immediate 'Good. Get me a hot towel' — as if the Jeannie call was never what he wanted, using Beverly's refusal as cover for his own ambivalence
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compressed character moment: Larry's emotional avoidance is so total that he uses Beverly's veto as an exit ramp, then pivots to a trivial comfort object (hot towel) as though nothing happened. The rapid transition is pure Larry Sanders. High economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Who can afford a hair weave or a transplant? And for that matter, who knows a baboon who wants to give you his hair?

jokes.text: Larry's extended spiral about hot towels: 'They're out there. You don't need to check. Artie was selling them like there's no tomorrow...' building to 'I'm going crazy. I hear Jeannie crying in my head.'
jokes.setup: Beverly says she'll check on the hot towels
jokes.punchline: Larry's increasingly frantic insistence that the hot towels must exist — ending with a non-sequitur emotional confession about hearing Jeannie crying — shows his anxiety bleeding into everything
jokes.explanation: The escalation from hot towel logistics to 'I hear Jeannie crying in my head' is a perfect Larry Sanders tonal shift. The joke is that he's using the hot towel question as a displacement activity for real grief, and the mask briefly slips. Character-integrated absurdist escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If it's Hank, why isn't Hank here? Hank has one line, and it's his name. You think he can do that without a rehearsal?

jokes.text: '[Crying] Poor Larry.' — Beverly mimics Jeannie crying in Larry's head
jokes.setup: Larry says 'I hear Jeannie crying in my head'
jokes.punchline: Beverly immediately performs a brief, sarcastic crying impression with 'Poor Larry' — she's not sympathetic, she's gently mocking his self-pity
jokes.explanation: A perfect two-word deflation. Beverly's 'Poor Larry' mocking-cry is the entire joke — it takes Larry's genuine self-pity and simply mirrors it back as absurd. Extremely economical, and Beverly's dry delivery (inferred) makes it land as the wry commentary of someone who's watched Larry's narcissism for years.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Isn't 'cap in a can' funnier?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Cap in a can. Ha! You're right! That's funnier. Cap in a can!

jokes.text: Hank's reaction to news of the divorce: 'I thought you were talking about the Emmy nominations.' / 'Oh, screw her!'
jokes.setup: Someone (Beverly) mentions Jeannie in a sad context, implying Jeannie was a good person
jokes.punchline: Hank thought they were discussing the Emmy nominations — revealing he was grieving the Emmy snub, not the marriage — and then his instant turn to 'Screw her!' once he understands shows his loyalty was always to Larry's career, not Jeannie
jokes.explanation: Sharp reversal — the misdirection of Hank grieving the nominations rather than the marriage is funny and character-revealing. 'Screw her!' snapping on instantly is perfectly Hank: performative loyalty covering genuine self-interest.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This doesn't look like it comes from a can. I understand how this part could come from a can, but how would the brim know to come out of the can before the rest of the hat?

jokes.text: Hank's anecdote: 'One time, one time I was invited to Larry's house while they were married.' — delivered as if this is a meaningful intimacy
jokes.setup: Hank is asserting his closeness to Larry in the wake of the divorce
jokes.punchline: The comedy is the inadvertent revelation of how infrequently he was welcome at Larry's home — 'one time, one time' — which he presents as evidence of their deep friendship
jokes.explanation: This is a perfectly calibrated Hank joke: the pathos of a man who has convinced himself that one home invitation constitutes deep friendship. The repetition of 'one time, one time' is both emphatic (his intention) and self-undermining (the joke). It simultaneously reveals the Larry/Hank relationship and Hank's delusional self-regard. Strong originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I'm pissing in my pants, conceptual flaw and all!

jokes.text: Hank's plan for the post-divorce period: 'We'd hit the bar at the Bel Air Hotel, work a little skirt.'
jokes.setup: Hank is fondly recalling the period between Larry's marriages when they were 'very tight'
jokes.punchline: 'Work a little skirt' — a grotesquely dated piece of predatory bro-speak from Hank that reveals how he views their friendship (primarily as a wing-man arrangement)
jokes.explanation: Hank's sleazy excitement about Larry being single again is funny for its transparency. 'Work a little skirt' is an anachronistic phrase even for 1993, which makes it character-revealing. Moderately strong.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: I'm sure that the writers can cook up something funny about your marital disorders.

jokes.text: 'I guess this year I'm going to get very, very close to Larry.' — Hank to Beverly, with apparent excitement
jokes.setup: Hank has been laying out how Jeannie always kept him at arm's length from Larry
jokes.punchline: Hank's naked eagerness — framing Larry's emotional devastation as a personal opportunity — is the joke; Beverly's presumably flat non-reaction amplifies it
jokes.explanation: A good character beat that caps Hank's monologue about Jeannie. The comedy is Hank's complete lack of awareness that his opportunism is visible. Character-integrated and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: He's been working on them since 1989.

jokes.text: 'Jerry Van Dyke. Fuck him.' — Larry's non-sequitur outburst, apparently upon seeing a name on the Emmy nominee list
jokes.setup: Larry is reading the Emmy nominations he claimed not to want to see
jokes.punchline: The sudden, furious 'Jerry Van Dyke. Fuck him.' — an explosion of specific resentment at a minor celebrity — is perfectly calibrated industry-insider petty jealousy
jokes.explanation: Four words that encapsulate the entire show's thesis about showbiz pettiness. 'Jerry Van Dyke' is the ideal choice — a real, recognizable, distinctly B-list celebrity, famous primarily as Dick Van Dyke's less-successful brother. The specificity is the joke: not a big star, not an obvious rival, just someone whose name triggers an existential rage in Larry. 'Fuck him.' is perfectly economical. This is among the best jokes in the episode — quotable, deeply character-integrated, and funny in a way that rewards insider knowledge without requiring it. Comparable to the 8+ anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No, no. Lee Marvin lost everything but the dog.

jokes.text: Larry to Melanie Parrish, repeating 'Artie's not here' three times as she tries to discuss real business
jokes.setup: Melanie Parrish from the network has come to Larry's office; Larry clearly doesn't want to deal with her
jokes.punchline: Larry keeps deflecting with 'Artie's not here' — treating Artie as a human shield — even as she explicitly says she came to see Larry
jokes.explanation: The running repetition of 'Artie's not here' as a deflection is very funny — it's Larry's anxiety made visible. He keeps restating it like a mantra even after it's been dismissed. Character-integrated and well-structured as a mini-running gag within the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It should with that hippie in the white house.

jokes.text: Melanie delivers the Phoenix affiliate news — 'They're dropping you for Chevy Chase' — then immediately says 'Hard to believe, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Melanie is informing Larry that Phoenix is dropping his show
jokes.punchline: 'Hard to believe, isn't it?' — ostensibly commiserating but with a tone that suggests it isn't actually that hard to believe. The Chevy Chase detail (a notoriously troubled TV endeavor) adds absurdity
jokes.explanation: The joke plays on the real-world knowledge that Chevy Chase's talk show was famously awful — being dropped FOR Chevy Chase is a specific and pointed insult. 'Hard to believe, isn't it?' is a good deadpan line. Gets a rewatch bonus because the Chevy Chase joke aged into a richer joke about how wrong Phoenix was.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What kind of bit? Two guys with patches on. Take it off.

jokes.text: Larry's paralyzed response to Kathy Ireland — shoe conversation: 'What do you think of my shoes?' / 'They're great. Open-toed. Mine are closed-toed—' / 'I like all your shoes.'
jokes.setup: Larry is meeting Kathy Ireland and clearly trying to make a good impression in front of Artie
jokes.punchline: He gets trapped in a shoe conversation he has no idea how to exit, leading to the bizarre non-compliment 'I like all your shoes' — a man who has never successfully flirted
jokes.explanation: Cringe comedy in the Larry Sanders mode — the joke is Larry's social incompetence with women he finds attractive. 'I like all your shoes' is the kind of desperate overreach that's cringingly recognizable. Works as character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Uh, she's almost housebroken.

jokes.text: 'I feel embarrassed talking about my photos. I have a new movie.' [Pause] 'The last paisan.' 'I saw it twice.' 'It's not out yet.' 'I hear you're wonderful.'
jokes.setup: Kathy Ireland arrives for her pre-show meeting with Larry
jokes.punchline: Larry claims to have seen her unreleased movie twice; she says it's not out yet; he pivots to 'I hear you're wonderful' — a perfect string of celebrity sycophancy exposed as lies
jokes.explanation: A brilliant sequence revealing the hollow mechanics of celebrity interview prep. Larry claims to have seen an unreleased movie twice, is caught, and immediately pivots to 'I hear you're wonderful' — the ultimate non-committal compliment. This is Larry Sanders at its most satirically sharp about the nature of the talk show relationship. The three-beat exposure structure is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It says, 'Have fun in Vegas.' I'm not going to Vegas.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes, you are.

jokes.text: 'Until we get this show on track, I have no dick.' / 'No dick? Check.'
jokes.setup: Artie suggests Larry should start dating, starting with Kathy Ireland
jokes.punchline: Larry's declaration of sexual dormancy for career reasons; Artie's instant 'No dick? Check.' — acknowledging it with the same professionalism as a production note
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'No dick? Check.' is a sublime comedy beat — the professionalism of 'Check' applied to Larry's announcement of sexual abstinence is perfectly absurd. It treats an intimate declaration like a production checklist item. The economy is exceptional: two words doing enormous work. Highly quotable. This ranks among the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I've seen men try to lose themselves in their work like this before-- Redd Foxx and Dick Shawn and Regis Philbin. Capisce?

jokes.text: Ratings discussion: 'Remember, Koppel had the Buttafuocos.' / 'Jesus, he's dipping into the toilet.' / 'I agree.' / 'Why didn't we get the Buttafuocos on?' / 'They turned us down.' / 'Good. They're not right for the show anyway.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are reviewing ratings; Artie uses Koppel's Buttafuoco booking as a ratings comparison
jokes.punchline: Larry condemns Koppel for booking trash guests, then immediately asks why they didn't get those same guests, then immediately reframes the rejection as a principled decision — a three-beat hypocrisy spiral
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional joke construction. In six rapid exchanges, we watch Larry's entire self-deception apparatus operate in real time: (1) condemn the lowbrow move, (2) immediately want to copy it, (3) learn you were rejected, (4) retroactively claim artistic integrity. The structural precision is remarkable — each beat lands and the final 'They're not right for the show anyway' is the perfect self-deluding button. This is among the best exchanges in the episode. Strong structure and character integration scores.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: But the best cure for stress is... Blow jobs. Bingo.

jokes.text: Hank's Vegas pitch: 'I'm meeting two lovely ladies at the Bel Air Hotel. There's two of them, one of me, so... No pressure.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank what he's doing after the show; Hank is attempting to invite Larry to a double date
jokes.punchline: 'There's two of them, one of me, so...' — the pause implying an obvious conclusion — followed by 'No pressure,' which undercuts the pitch entirely, suggesting Hank himself isn't sure this is a good idea
jokes.explanation: Hank's hapless matchmaking is classic character comedy. 'No pressure' lands because it contradicts the whole thrust of the pitch. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What a little kiss-ass.

jokes.text: Hank's hair transplant monologue: 'Who can afford a hair weave or a transplant? And for that matter, who knows a baboon who wants to give you his hair?'
jokes.setup: Hank has segued into what is apparently an on-air monologue about hair loss solutions
jokes.punchline: 'Who knows a baboon who wants to give you his hair?' — an absurdist escalation from practical options to an impossible one, with the baboon liver transplant reference right after confirming the topical (and self-deprecating, given Hank's own hair) setup
jokes.explanation: An on-air segment joke — this is technically Hank performing on the show-within-the-show. The baboon escalation is mildly absurdist and self-deprecating given Hank's own follicular situation, but the joke is fairly thin. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Bob Stevens. Who's Bob Stevens? Bob Stevens is an ordinary, everyday guy.

jokes.text: 'That's going to be Hank.' / 'If it's Hank, why isn't Hank here?' / 'Hank has one line, and it's his name. You think he can do that without a rehearsal?'
jokes.setup: They're rehearsing the 'cap in a can' bit; a stand-in is playing Hank
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'You think he can do that without a rehearsal?' is devastatingly precise: the joke is that Hank's contribution to the bit is literally saying his own name, yet the question is whether he needs preparation for this
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest Hank burns. The logic of 'his one line is his own name' perfectly encapsulates Hank's diminished role and Larry's contempt for him — and the rhetorical question 'You think he can do that without a rehearsal?' adds a second layer by actually acknowledging Hank might need the rehearsal. Deep character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well... This is really going to sell.

jokes.text: 'Isn't Cap in a Can funnier than Hat in a Can?' / 'Cap in a can. Ha! You're right! That's funnier. Cap in a can!'
jokes.setup: They're rehearsing a bit about a spray-on hair product called 'Hat in a Can'
jokes.punchline: Larry's in-the-moment suggestion ('Cap in a can') is instantly adopted with disproportionate enthusiasm — the comedy writers workshopping their own mediocre bit in real time
jokes.explanation: A meta moment — we're watching the show's writers room process, and the bit they're so excited about is itself quite mediocre, which is part of the joke. Moderate execution.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Bob, I guess you're pretty sold on this product. Aren't you, Bob? Bob? Hank? Yeah.

jokes.text: 'How would the brim know to come out of the can before the rest of the hat?' / 'Are you actually questioning the reality of this?' / 'If I don't, who will?'
jokes.setup: They're looking at a comically ill-fitting hat from a can that doesn't look like it could come from a can
jokes.punchline: Larry's literal-minded interrogation of the impossible product logic ('how would the brim know?') followed by his earnest defense of his own pedantry — 'If I don't, who will?'
jokes.explanation: The joke lands because Larry's insistence on interrogating the physical logic of a comedy prop is both absurdist and perfectly in character — this is a man who cannot switch off his critical faculties even in the middle of a stupid bit. 'If I don't, who will?' is a great line. Artie's 'I'm pissing in my pants' (then following it) is a nice physical comedy button too.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You can't buy those kind of fuck-ups, Larry.

jokes.text: 'I'm pissing in my pants, conceptual flaw and all!'
jokes.setup: Larry has just raised the legitimate structural flaw in the 'cap in a can' prop
jokes.punchline: Artie's enthusiastic endorsement despite fully acknowledging the flaw — 'conceptual flaw and all' — is a producer choosing commercial viability over logic, which is very Artie
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'pissing in my pants, conceptual flaw and all!' is a great line. The 'conceptual flaw and all' acknowledgment is the key — he's not ignoring the problem, he's cheerfully embracing it. Very Artie: pragmatic about everything, including the inadequacy of his own ideas.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Let's book Boy George. His smack problems are behind him.

jokes.text: Artie on how many divorce jokes he has: 'A couple.' / 'How many?' / '200.' / 'He's been working on them since 1989.'
jokes.setup: Artie claimed he has 'a couple' divorce jokes prepared
jokes.punchline: He actually has 200, and someone reveals he's been writing them since 1989 — implying Artie anticipated this divorce four years before it happened, suggesting either prescience or participation in its cause
jokes.explanation: A great escalation joke: 'a couple' to 200 is one level, but 'since 1989' transforms it into something much darker — Artie has been prepared for this specific outcome for years. The comedy is in the implication: either Artie knew, or he wanted it. Rewatch bonus because it rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You ever feel like somebody grabbed you, when they weren't there?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That was weird.

jokes.text: Jeannie's legal restraining order against Larry making any jokes about her on the show
jokes.setup: Beverly delivers a legal document: Jeannie has obtained a court order preventing Larry from joking about her
jokes.punchline: The absurdity of a legal instrument against comedy, combined with the devastating practical effect — it eliminates Artie's 200 jokes and Larry's best monologue material
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-specific satirical beat: the idea that a comedy writer's personal life could be legally protected from becoming material is very specific to the world of late-night. Callbacks to Artie's 200 jokes (now worthless) adds craft.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That's a heart attack.

jokes.text: 'I recognize this stationery.' — Larry's response to Jeannie's legal document
jokes.setup: Beverly hands Larry the restraining order
jokes.punchline: Rather than processing the legal content, Larry recognizes — and comments on — the stationery, suggesting this isn't the first time he's received frightening legal documents on this particular paper
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent beat. The specificity of recognizing the stationery suggests a whole history of legal threats — and that Larry has processed them enough to catalog the paper. It's a small absurdist detail that lands as deadpan character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I first met Larry in the spring of 1985. My cruise liner was moored off the coast of portugal. Amen.

jokes.text: 'I won't even get the dog.' / 'No, no. Lee Marvin lost everything but the dog.'
jokes.setup: Larry bemoans not getting the dog in the divorce settlement, referencing Marvin Mitchelson (famous palimony attorney)
jokes.punchline: Artie corrects him: it's Lee Marvin (the actor in the famous palimony case, not Marvin Mitchelson) — the word 'Marvin' confused him — and notes Lee Marvin actually kept the dog, so even that precedent doesn't apply
jokes.explanation: An insider legal/celebrity reference joke that rewards cultural knowledge (the famous Lee Marvin palimony case). Artie's correction of Larry's muddled Marvin confusion is efficient and funny. Works best for viewers who know the reference.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank? Ge the fuck off the bed.

jokes.text: Artie's son has been arrested for possession; Artie immediately says: 'Call my lawyer. I hope bail becomes tax-deductible. It should with that hippie in the White House.'
jokes.setup: Artie's assistant whispers that his son Eddie has been arrested for drug possession
jokes.punchline: Artie's priorities are: (1) lawyer, (2) tax implications of bail, (3) blaming Clinton — all before any parental concern registers
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Artie. His response to his son's arrest is entirely logistical and political — zero emotional register, 100% pragmatic. 'I hope bail becomes tax-deductible' is a beautiful line: the specificity of using a crisis as a tax strategy reveals an entire psychology. 'With that hippie in the White House' adds a political dimension that's perfectly consistent with Artie's worldview. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You're 42. Don't push so hard.

jokes.text: Larry reading the Letterman quote aloud: 'I'm not the kind of person who wants to see somebody else fail on television... I'm in pretty good shape.'
jokes.setup: Larry reads a Letterman quote that is passive-aggressive in the guise of magnanimity
jokes.punchline: The irony operates on two levels: Letterman is obviously gloating while claiming not to care, and Larry reads it straight while clearly being devastated by it
jokes.explanation: Works as context-building for Larry's Letterman obsession. The Letterman quote is itself funny in its passive aggression. But this beat is more setup than punchline — it prepares a running thread.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This heart attack is a warning. It was a heart episode.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: You know what I mean.

jokes.text: Hank enters wearing an eye patch — 'I figured if I wore a patch, it won't look odd that you have one on. People will think it's a bit.'
jokes.setup: Larry has an eye patch due to his eye condition (mentioned earlier: 'his eye is leaking like Niagara Falls'); Hank enters with an identical patch
jokes.punchline: Hank's logic — preemptive mimicry to normalize Larry's medical patch as a planned comedic bit — is both touching and spectacularly misguided. His solution to Larry's embarrassment is to make it weirder.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's finest character moments. Hank's plan to solve Larry's problem by copying his medical condition — so 'it looks like a bit' — is an act of both sincere solidarity and profound stupidity. The logic is internally consistent but completely wrong, which is Hank at his best. 'What kind of bit? / Two guys with patches on.' is a hilarious micro-exchange. High originality and character integration — this is uniquely Hank, nobody else would think of this or execute it with this earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: And she took the dog.

jokes.text: 'What kind of bit?' / 'Two guys with patches on.' / 'Take it off.'
jokes.setup: Larry demands to know what bit would involve two guys wearing eye patches
jokes.punchline: Hank's entirely undefended description of the 'bit' — 'two guys with patches on' — as though the concept is self-evidently funny, followed by Larry's flat 'Take it off'
jokes.explanation: The micro-exchange after the eye patch reveal is even funnier than the reveal itself. Hank's confident description of his 'bit' — 'two guys with patches on' — as a full justification is perfectly absurd. The complete absence of any other concept is the joke. 'Take it off.' is the ideal button: three syllables of total dismissal.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Before you know it, your head turns sideways, you're coughing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm just gonna go fuck myself.

jokes.text: Hank presents a puppy with the inscription 'Have fun in Vegas'
jokes.setup: Hank says he has a heartfelt get-well gift for Larry; there is an emotional setup, a box is presented
jokes.punchline: The gift is a puppy — thoughtful — but the inscription reads 'Have fun in Vegas,' revealing Hank's actual agenda: the gift is a Trojan horse for a Vegas trip pitch. He didn't even get a condolence inscription.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed character comedy moment. The emotional buildup ('It just breaks my heart what this woman is doing to you'), the gift reveal (a puppy — sweet), then the inscription ('Have fun in Vegas') — each beat subverts the previous one. It perfectly captures Hank's character: genuine affection that is always ultimately in service of his own agenda. The inscription reveal is the precise kind of multi-layered character comedy that marks the show's best writing.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Stress kills, you know? And-- and we all know, the best relief in the world for stress is--

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Don't say it, Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Blowjobs.

jokes.text: Hank's advice: 'Redd Foxx and Dick Shawn and Regis Philbin' as examples of men who tried to lose themselves in their work
jokes.setup: Hank is cautioning Larry against overworking as a coping mechanism
jokes.punchline: Hank's list of cautionary examples — Redd Foxx (died of a heart attack on set), Dick Shawn (died on stage), Regis Philbin — the first two are dead men, making Regis Philbin as a final example absurdly bathetic; also, Redd Foxx literally died of a heart attack, which is Larry's current situation
jokes.explanation: This is exquisitely calibrated dark comedy. Redd Foxx and Dick Shawn both famously died while performing (Foxx of a heart attack, Shawn collapsed on stage) — so Hank's list of people who worked themselves to death is accidentally/ignorantly pointing directly at Larry's present heart scare. Regis Philbin as the third name deflates into the mundane, which is the structural joke. The dark irony of invoking men who literally died on the job while warning someone about a heart episode earns this a high score.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: Is that anything like a designing women episode?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yes, in that they both make you sick?

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: Yes, and involve fatty build-up.

jokes.text: Hank's cure for stress: 'The best cure for stress is...' [pause] 'Blow jobs.'
jokes.setup: Hank is building to his supposedly wise medical advice about stress management
jokes.punchline: 'Blow jobs' — delivered with apparent sincerity as a medical solution
jokes.explanation: A decent Hank joke — the buildup and earnest delivery make it funnier than the content alone warrants. But 'blow jobs as medical advice' is a fairly standard comedy beat. Gets a callback bonus because it's repeated later.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Most people are mad at me.

jokes.text: Paul Shaffer quote: 'I don't care where Dave goes, as long as I go with him.' Larry: 'What a little kiss-ass.'
jokes.setup: Larry is reading Letterman coverage, this time a Paul Shaffer loyalty quote
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'What a little kiss-ass' — the contempt is funny partly because Larry would absolutely say the same thing about Artie if the situation were reversed, and partly because calling Paul Shaffer a 'little kiss-ass' is perfectly calibrated industry-insider cattiness
jokes.explanation: Good Larry character beat — his contempt for Shaffer's loyalty is ironic given his own need for sycophantic support. Efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wow, if your back end gets too big, you gotta get a Stairmaster.

jokes.text: Artie's direction to cameraman: 'No more tight shots of Larry, goddamnit. His eye is leaking like Niagara Falls. Stay wide. Stay wide.'
jokes.setup: The show is taping; Artie is in the control room managing the production
jokes.punchline: 'His eye is leaking like Niagara Falls' — a comically vivid production note that doubles as a brutal assessment of Larry's physical state
jokes.explanation: 'Leaking like Niagara Falls' is a great image — Artie's production instincts firing even as Larry is physically deteriorating. The fact that 'stay wide' is the solution to a medical symptom is funny. Good economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: This is 8 ball in the corner pocket. This is game over. All we need are our cue sticks, it sounds like to me. Hey, now. You bring the chalk.

jokes.text: After the cap-in-a-can spray, the subject Bob Stevens sits there with a hilariously bad spray-hair result; Larry says 'Well... This is really going to sell.'
jokes.setup: Larry has sprayed the product on Bob; the result is apparently terrible
jokes.punchline: 'This is really going to sell.' — deadpan, watching a product demonstration that has clearly gone wrong
jokes.explanation: A good on-air deadpan. The visual of a bad spray-hair result is the setup; Larry's sarcastic confidence is the button. Economy is the strength here.

jokes.text: Larry calls out 'Bob? Hank? Yeah.' — the bit trails off with Bob apparently unable to respond and Hank stepping in with nothing
jokes.setup: Larry tries to wrap up the cap-in-a-can segment by asking 'Bob' for his reaction
jokes.punchline: Bob doesn't respond; Larry pivots to Hank; Hank's entire contribution is 'Yeah'; applause follows — the whole bit is a sequence of collapsed communication that somehow works
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff: Artie said Hank's entire contribution was his name; here Hank's contribution is literally just 'Yeah.' The bit's awkward collapse — an empty response from Bob, a monosyllabic non-contribution from Hank — and the audience applauding anyway is a perfect encapsulation of late-night fakery. Rewatch bonus because it pays off the earlier rehearsal joke.

jokes.text: 'You can't buy those kind of fuck-ups, Larry. You hear the audience? What do you want?'
jokes.setup: Coming offstage after the cap-in-a-can bit, which was chaotic
jokes.punchline: Artie's reframing of the bit's failure as a success — 'You can't buy those kind of fuck-ups' — is a producer's instinct to spin any result as the intended outcome
jokes.explanation: 'You can't buy those kind of fuck-ups' is a highly quotable, deeply character-integrated Artie line. It encapsulates his philosophy: in live television, a clean failure is as valuable as a clean success, because the audience loves authenticity — even accidental authenticity. The confidence in the spin is the joke. Strong economy.

jokes.text: 'Let's book Boy George. His smack problems are behind him.'
jokes.setup: Los Lobos is performing; Larry and Artie are watching from the wings
jokes.punchline: Larry's casual booking suggestion casually dismisses Boy George's well-documented heroin addiction as a resolved matter — the breezy confidence of 'behind him' makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: 'His smack problems are behind him' is a great showbiz line — the absolute confidence of a man who has no idea if this is true but needs the booking. The casual minimization of a serious addiction as a solved business inconvenience is dark and very funny.

jokes.text: Larry's chest pain during the Los Lobos performance: 'You ever feel like somebody grabbed you, when they weren't there?'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are enjoying the show; Larry seems to be having a good time for the first time all episode
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a moment of actual happiness, Larry describes cardiac symptoms in a confused, almost child-like way — the gap between the poetic description and the medical reality is darkly funny
jokes.explanation: The line 'somebody grabbed you, when they weren't there' is both the darkest line in the episode and unexpectedly funny in its dreamy vagueness. Artie's 'No. That was weird.' followed by the immediate 'That's a heart attack' is the perfect two-beat response: first confusion, then alarming clarity. The episode's dramatic turn is set up with a genuinely funny/horrifying exchange.

jokes.text: Hank's bedside prayer: 'We thank thee for sparing the life of Larry Sanders. I first met Larry in the spring of 1985. My cruise liner was moored off the coast of Portugal. Amen.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been hospitalized after his cardiac episode; Hank is apparently saying a prayer at his bedside
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'prayer' immediately pivots to a personal anecdote about meeting Larry — recasting religious gratitude as an opportunity to tell a self-aggrandizing story involving a cruise liner. 'Amen' lands at the end of what was clearly a personal story, not a prayer.
jokes.explanation: This is the single best joke in the episode and one of the finest Hank Kingsley moments in the series. The structure is perfect: a solemn opening ('We thank thee for sparing the life of Larry Sanders') that modulates from sincere to absurd the instant Hank inserts himself — turning a prayer for Larry's survival into a story about Hank's cruise ship. 'My cruise liner was moored off the coast of Portugal' is perhaps the most Hank sentence imaginable: specific, irrelevant, self-romanticizing, and somehow completely sincere. The 'Amen' button is structurally flawless. This is Tambor-level character comedy writing — it's about Hank's bottomless self-centeredness, but it's so specific and strange that it transcends simple narcissism jokes. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor in character integration.

jokes.text: Larry, waking from his hospital bed, first words: 'Get the fuck off the bed.'
jokes.setup: Larry is recovering; Hank has apparently gotten onto the hospital bed or is physically too close
jokes.punchline: Larry's first words after a near-death experience are a blunt expletive telling Hank to get away from him — no gratitude, no vulnerability, immediate return to form
jokes.explanation: Five words that tell you everything about Larry Sanders. After a cardiac episode, his first waking thought is to get Hank off his bed. There's no transformation, no softening — just immediate, uncomplicated Larry. The economy is exceptional. It's also a perfect button on Hank's cruise-liner prayer — all that sentiment answered with pure dismissal. This is what the show does best: character comedy so compressed it feels inevitable.

jokes.text: Hank says 'I'd like a moment alone with Beverly, please.' Larry: 'He wants a moment alone with Beverly.' / Hank: 'Hank, I heard what he said.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants private time with his assistant Beverly in the hospital room; people are being cleared out
jokes.punchline: Hank repeats Larry's request back to the room as if he's Larry's spokesman/announcer; when someone (Beverly) acknowledges hearing it, Hank doubles down with his own name — a non-sequitur assertion of presence
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Hank's automatic impulse to perform even in a hospital room. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'Racquetball, two weeks.' — Artie's post-cardiac-episode prescription for Larry
jokes.setup: Artie is encouraging Larry that he looks good
jokes.punchline: His idea of a recovery timeline is announcing Larry will be playing racquetball in two weeks — replacing the earlier 'walk it off' advice with only slightly more realistic sports medicine
jokes.explanation: A callback to Artie's 'walk it off' philosophy — now applied to a literal cardiac episode. 'Racquetball, two weeks' is a wonderfully economical callback that makes the earlier joke land harder in retrospect.

jokes.text: 'This heart attack is a warning.' / 'It was a heart episode.' / 'You know what I mean.' / 'I'm 40 years old.' / 'You're 42.'
jokes.setup: Larry is having a moment of genuine reflection about his life
jokes.punchline: Every attempt at self-dramatization is punctured by Beverly: 'heart episode' not 'heart attack'; '42' not '40' — Beverly's flat accuracy deflates Larry's attempts to construct his own narrative
jokes.explanation: Beverly as reality-checker is pitch-perfect. The two corrections — medical terminology and age — are both delivered without sympathy, and both are exactly what Larry needs and doesn't want. '42' is funnier than it should be. The rhythm of these quick exchanges is very well-crafted.

jokes.text: The dog: Larry says 'I want it. Get the dog.' / Beverly: 'Jeannie stopped by... And she took the dog.'
jokes.setup: Larry, in a moment of post-cardiac sentimentality, decides the dog would make him happy
jokes.punchline: Jeannie has just taken the dog — the one comforting thing he reached for has been removed right before he asks for it; the timing is perfect cruelty
jokes.explanation: The timing is the entire joke — Larry reaches for the one tender thing, and it's already gone. Beverly's delivery ('She stopped by... And she took the dog') is structured to land the news after a beat. The comedy and sadness are inseparable here; it's the show's signature tonal blend. Structurally very well executed.

jokes.text: 'Is that anything like a Designing Women episode?' / 'Yes, in that they both make you sick?' / 'Yes, and involve fatty build-up.'
jokes.setup: Staff members are celebrating Larry's return; someone notes his 'heart episode' terminology
jokes.punchline: The Designing Women riff — a TV writers' room joke about a TV writers' room — culminating in 'fatty build-up' as an attribute shared by the show and cardiac disease
jokes.explanation: A tight three-beat exchange with genuine wordplay. 'Fatty build-up' as a linking term between cardiac disease and Designing Women is an unexpected and well-constructed punchline. The escalation structure (both make you sick → both involve fatty build-up) works as a comedic ladder.

jokes.text: 7.5 pounds of get-well cards vs. Hank's earlier broken leg getting 9 pounds: 'Last year when I broke my leg, didn't I get 9 pounds?' / 'Yes, but you've got 2 miles of faxes out there.'
jokes.setup: Larry's staff is celebrating 7.5 pounds of get-well cards
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately converts this from a celebration into a competition — his broken leg outperformed Larry's cardiac episode by 1.5 pounds of mail, making the metric itself absurd
jokes.explanation: A superb Hank moment. The idea of measuring fan affection in pounds — and Hank instantly recognizing the competitive implications — reveals his character perfectly. Beverly's smooth deflection ('Yes, but you've got 2 miles of faxes') shows she's done this before. 'Pounds of get-well cards' as a metric is inherently absurd and funny. Very strong character integration.

jokes.text: Larry dictating how get-well responses should be signed: 'Should I put Best wishes or Thanks for caring?' / 'Ah, your choice.' / 'Beverly, please.' / 'Oh, leave him be, Beverly.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to send personally autographed photos to everyone who sent a get-well card
jokes.punchline: The insistence on 'personally autographed' photos (i.e., having someone else sign them) for thousands of people, then agonizing over the inscription — the performative personal touch that is entirely impersonal — is classic Larry vanity
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Larry's narcissism expressed through the grammar of gratitude. The agonized choice between two equally meaningless phrases is funny. Artie's protective 'Leave him be' adds a nice layer.

jokes.text: 'But you've got 2 miles of faxes out there.' / 'Well, all right.' — Larry immediately consoled by the fax metric beating the card metric
jokes.setup: Hank is 'winning' the get-well-card competition with 9 pounds to Larry's 7½
jokes.punchline: Beverly reveals Larry has 2 miles of faxes — a new unit — and Larry is instantly comforted
jokes.explanation: A nice button on the get-well card bit. The measuring unit escalation (pounds → miles) is absurd in a good way, and Larry's instant 'Well, all right' upon learning he's ahead is perfect — he shouldn't care about this, but he does.

jokes.text: Larry's flattery to Helen Hunt: 'I think the viewing public is watching because they're Mad about you.' / 'Thank you very much.' / 'I personally think most people are mad about you.' / 'No — most, uh, most people are mad at me.'
jokes.setup: Larry makes a pun on Helen Hunt's show title 'Mad About You' as a compliment
jokes.punchline: Helen Hunt corrects him with the self-deprecating alternate reading — people are mad AT her — which is both humble and funnier than the compliment
jokes.explanation: A clean setup/punchline pun that works because Helen Hunt plays the turn well. The wordplay (mad about vs. mad at) is not especially original but is structurally sound and economical. The self-deprecation gives it warmth.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air interview with Helen Hunt about Mad About You: 'He has a dog and I have a neurotic sister and we both have jobs and somehow in there... Mad About You.'
jokes.setup: Helen Hunt describes her show Mad About You in the interview
jokes.punchline: Her description sounds deliberately generic — 'somehow in there, Mad About You' — as if she's not sure how her show happened either
jokes.explanation: This reads as a mild self-deprecating moment from Helen Hunt — acknowledging her show's premise is thin by trailing off into the title. Mild comedy, mostly functions as realistic talk-show content simulation.

jokes.text: 'I personally think that most people are mad about you.' / 'No. Most people are mad AT me.' [Laughter]
jokes.setup: Larry flatters Helen Hunt by saying 'most people are mad about you'
jokes.punchline: Helen corrects him — 'most people are mad at me' — a show-title pun that flips the sentiment from adoration to anger
jokes.explanation: A competent wordplay joke on 'mad about' vs. 'mad at' — the show title pun. It's the kind of joke a talk-show host would actually use. The delivery within the show-within-a-show context makes it feel authentic rather than hacky. Works as simulation of late-night banter but not remarkable writing.

jokes.text: 'Wow, if your back end gets too big, you gotta get a Stairmaster.'
jokes.setup: Helen Hunt says the show could add more episodes 'on the back end'
jokes.punchline: Larry takes 'back end' literally — as a reference to a physical backside — and makes a Stairmaster exercise joke
jokes.explanation: A weak on-air joke — the double-entendre on 'back end' is the kind of lowest-common-denominator wordplay that dates badly. It's also characteristically poor late-night interview banter, which could be the meta-joke (showing Larry making a mediocre joke on air), but it's too weak even for that reading.

jokes.text: Larry asks about Helen Hunt's Hawaii story, then abruptly cuts to commercial when she starts telling it: 'Hey, why don't you hold that thought, and I'll be right back.'
jokes.setup: Larry sets up Helen Hunt's Hawaii story as something worth exploring ('was there a funny story?')
jokes.punchline: The instant she starts to tell it, he cuts her off for commercial — revealing that his interest was entirely performative; the commercial break is more valuable than her story
jokes.explanation: A meta-comment on the late-night interview format: the host sets up the story precisely to have it cut off by commercial, which is structurally revealing about how these shows work. Larry's 'okay, see you in a minute' and Helen Hunt's flat 'No flipping. You're a riot' — said without conviction — is a nice button.

jokes.text: Larry loses track of the interview: 'How was your fish? It's a little dry.' — completely random tangent mid-interview
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to get to a funny Hawaii story from the pre-interview, asks about the new time slot
jokes.punchline: 'How was your fish? It's a little dry.' — Larry goes completely off-script, apparently asking about dinner/lunch in the middle of a live interview, and answers his own question
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. Larry's mind clearly wandered — 'How was your fish?' has nothing to do with any topic — and he answers his own question ('It's a little dry'). This is perfect Larry Sanders behavior: the professional incompetence masked by smooth delivery. The non sequitur is so committed that it reads as simultaneously confused and confident. Very specific and quotable.

jokes.text: Larry's post-show assessment of Helen Hunt: 'All she talked about was show business, and all I did was pretend to be interested.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are debriefing after Helen Hunt's interview
jokes.punchline: Larry's complaint that she talked about show business — while he himself has talked about nothing but show business all episode — is ironic self-unawareness
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — Larry accusing a guest of talking about show business is rich given the episode's content. Efficient but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Hank's Disney waitress pitch: 'They drove in all the way from Anaheim... do you think they wanna drive all the way back there tonight? ... After all, that is a 2-hour drive.' / 'I think that's just to the monorail stop, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Hank is pitching two female Disney employees as potential companions for the night
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'I think that's just to the monorail stop' — quietly devastating the logic of Hank's '2-hour drive' argument with geographic specificity
jokes.explanation: Larry's Disneyland geography correction is a quietly brilliant line — it punctures Hank's seduction logic with the kind of pedantic precision that is very much Larry's mode. 'The monorail stop' is funnier than it needs to be. The specificity elevates it.

jokes.text: 'Maybe just as well it didn't go anywhere.' / 'I won't book her anymore.'
jokes.setup: Artie tries to console Larry about the failed Helen Hunt interview chemistry
jokes.punchline: Larry's response to the suggestion it's 'just as well' — 'I won't book her anymore' — is a petty blacklisting response that treats a minor professional awkwardness as grounds for career exclusion
jokes.explanation: Larry's industry power expressed as petty revenge. 'I won't book her anymore' as a response to a slightly dull interview is a good character beat — revealing how show hosts actually operate. The pettiness is perfectly Larry.

jokes.text: Hank's closing pitch: 'Two lovely ladies from Anaheim, Disney employees, waitresses. The Dumbo Hilton — the Dumbo Hyatt — I don't know.' / [Both] 'Bel Air Hotel!'
jokes.setup: Hank has two Disney employees from Anaheim he's trying to set up for a double date after the show
jokes.punchline: He can't remember whether they're at the Dumbo Hilton or the Dumbo Hyatt — neither of which exists — and both Larry and Artie finish his sentence with 'Bel Air Hotel' in unison
jokes.explanation: The Bel Air Hotel callback pays off in the best possible way: both men say it simultaneously, revealing it's so established in their shared world that it requires no thought. The 'Dumbo Hilton/Dumbo Hyatt' confusion is a nice bit — Hank can't remember the hotel name but knows it's in Anaheim, at least. A satisfying episode-closer joke that lands on the show's repeated location gag.

jokes.text: Hank's 'Bel Air Hotel' callback and 8-ball metaphor: 'Larry, this is 8 ball in the corner pocket. This is game over. All we need are our cue sticks.' / 'You bring the chalk.'
jokes.setup: Hank is using billiards metaphors to describe the certainty of their success with the Disney waitresses
jokes.punchline: 'You bring the chalk' — Larry's participation in Hank's metaphor suggests he's been talked into it; the verbal Bel Air Hotel running gag pays off
jokes.explanation: The Bel Air Hotel has been Hank's recurring solution to all problems throughout the episode; this is its final invocation. Larry's 'You bring the chalk' — complete buy-in through a strained pool metaphor — is a good button. Rewatch bonus as the culmination of the running Bel Air/Hank companion thread.

jokes.text: Hank's blow jobs callback: 'The best relief in the world for stress is—' / 'Don't say it, Hank.' / 'Blowjobs.' / 'Main floor, talk show. Think about it.'
jokes.setup: Hank is back on his stress-relief speech, as Larry returns to work
jokes.punchline: Larry's preemptive 'Don't say it, Hank' — proving he knows exactly what's coming — followed by Hank saying it anyway, then the elevator announcement ('Main floor, talk show') as a deadpan button
jokes.explanation: The callback works because Larry's 'Don't say it, Hank' shows he's heard this before (we also heard it), and Hank says it anyway — confirming it's compulsive rather than strategic. 'Main floor, talk show' from the elevator as a button is an excellent bit of structure — the show reasserting itself over Hank's advice.

tmdb_overview: Larry is a wreck as he faces sinking ratings, no Emmy nominations, and a divorce suit from Jeannie. So Hank and Artie try to fix him up with attractive women. But the only one he really connects with is Francine, his first wife.
